query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A pre‐treatment that enriches the surface of a boride-based component with hafnium—so that upon exposure to high temperature it forms a dense, continuous HfO2 layer—will reduce molten‐aluminum corrosion compared to untreated components.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard boride-based parts (e.g., conventional metal diborides or high-entropy boride ceramics) prepared by conventional methods and lacking a hafnium-enriched surface layer.
generation.intervention: Apply a high-temperature surface treatment (e.g., a controlled thin hafnium deposition and subsequent short-term sintering) that promotes Hf diffusion into the near-surface region so that, during service, Hf oxidizes to form an adherent HfO2 barrier.
generation.conditions: The treatment is effective for components operating in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment where exposure to molten aluminum at temperatures around 700–800 °C is typical, and under cyclic thermal conditions representative of plating operations.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a cohesive, Hf-rich transitional layer that, upon oxidation, develops into a continuous, dense HfO2 scale acting as a physical and chemical barrier.
generation.mechanism: Hafnium has a high affinity for oxygen and forms a very stable, refractory oxide. With the enriched surface, Hf preferentially oxidizes under operational conditions to produce a protective HfO2 layer. This oxide reduces oxygen and aluminum atom diffusion between the molten aluminum and the underlying boride, thereby hindering corrosion and degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated components, the hafnium-surface-treated parts should exhibit lower weight-change rates (or less spallation) when immersed in molten aluminum and maintain a more intact, less corroded surface after prolonged exposure. Improvements may be evident as a substantial reduction in corrosion-related mass loss and microstructural damage.
generation.baseline: Boride components without any hafnium enrichment or surface pre-treatment, which typically develop less protective oxide scales and show higher corrosion rates in molten aluminum environments.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to remain effective as long as the HfO2 layer remains continuous and adherent; if the pre-treatment does not uniformly enrich the surface or if operating temperatures or rapid thermal cycling cause mechanical spallation of the oxide, the protection may degrade. Additionally, the benefit is assumed for conditions typical of hot-dip aluminum plating (around 700–800 °C) and may not extrapolate to significantly higher or more aggressive chemical environments.
generation.uncertainty: The hypothesis combines findings from studies showing that (1) high-entropy borides with a greater fraction of refractory elements such as Hf and Zr have improved oxidation resistance (PMC10608203::web::018::5_conclusions, PMC5126569::web::013::hardness_and_oxidation_resistance) and (2) Hf coatings on HEA substrates form protective HfO2 layers that reduce oxidation (PMC10488483::web::016::4_conclusions). The extension of these results to molten-aluminum corrosion protection is new and untested, and the magnitude of improvement and long-term adherence of the oxide under cyclic conditions remain to be validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of boride-based components: one set receiving a controlled surface treatment to enrich with hafnium (via thin-film deposition followed by a high-temperature diffusion step) and a control set with no treatment. Expose both sets to molten aluminum in a laboratory furnace maintained at ~750 °C for varying durations. After exposure, analyze the surfaces using weight measurements, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to assess oxide layer formation and corrosion extent.
measurements: Mass change (weight gain/loss) after molten aluminum exposure
Surface and cross-sectional microstructure and oxide layer morphology via SEM/EDS
Quantitative analysis of oxide composition (e.g., presence of HfO2 versus less protective oxides)
Electrochemical impedance or other corrosion metrics if applicable
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hafnium-treated components do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in corrosion indicators (e.g., similar weight change, irregular or discontinuous oxide layer, or similar damage extent) compared to the untreated controls, then the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-temperature oxidation-resistant VZrHfNbTa refractory HEA-based Hf-coated composites are prepared by the combined process. It has a coating thickness of 120 μm. Vanadium, niobium, tantalum and hafnium elements in the base alloy have obvious boundaries with the hafnium coating, and the zirconium element undergoes diffusion and migration in the coating with a diffusive distance of about 60 μm. High-temperature oxidation tests show that the weight gain per unit area of the coated sample is much less than that of the uncoated sample. Dents and pulverization on the surface of the alloy after oxidation of the uncoated specimen, oxidation, and sintering on the surface of the coated specimen result in the formation of a dense HfO2 protective layer. The coating can effectively improve the oxidation resistance of the material in extreme environments and prevent the surface from chalking, thus extending the material’s service life and broadening the application. The paper presents the results of obtaining single-phase high-entropy ceramic materials with a high degree of chemical homogeneity using the equiatomic high-entropy boride (TiZrHfTaNb)B2 as an example. Single-phase and chemically homogeneous high-entropy borides were obtained by preliminary mixing of metals at the atomic level. The results of process research of mechanical alloying of TiZrHfTaNb showed that a homogeneous chemical composition with the lowest iron content (0.12%) was achieved with the following mechanical alloying modes: a rotation of the planetary disk/pots was 200–400 rpm and a process time was of 7.5 h. During sintering at temperatures around 1600 °C, a high-entropy boride with the chemical formula MeB2 is formed. Inclusions in the form of zirconium-hafnium oxide and a transition layer between oxide inclusions and the main boride phase are formed on the surface. Increasing the process temperature to 2000 °C leads to the formation of single-phase and chemically homogeneous high-entropy boride (TiZrHfTaNb)B2.
